newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. sues tobacco companies, had talks with industry.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. sues tobacco companies, had talks with industry.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

New York state's attorney general sued the tobacco industry Monday in the first case seeking the dissolution of two of its research groups, alleging they are merely a publicity front for cigarette makers.

New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco also revealed he had proposed last year that the industry pay the state $656 million to head off the lawsuit and said cigarette makers responded with a "laughable" counteroffer of less than $5 million.
Lucia Valente, chief special counsel to Vacco, told Reuters that she believed New York was the first state to offer a proposal directly to the tobacco industry.
The lawsuit also accuses the companies of allegedly "illegally luring teenagers into smoking cigarettes".

The defendants named in the lawsuit include R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, a division of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.; Philip Morris Cos. Inc.; Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., which is owned by B.A.T Industries Plc; Loews Corp.'s Lorillard Tobacco Co.; and Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group Inc.

R.J. Reynolds Tobacco spokeswoman Peggy Carter said while company officials had met with Vacco's staff to explain why they thought there would be no merit to his lawsuit, there was no discussion of a settlement or proposals involving money.
"We've had no conversations like this," she said.

Tom Fitzgerald, a spokesman for Brown & Williamson, said the company believed the New York suit was without merit and would fight it. He also denied the company had any settlement talks with the attorney general.
"There have been no negotiations with representatives from Brown & Williamson," he said.

Vacco is the the 19th state attorney general to sue the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers. Alabama's lieutentant governor also filed a private lawsuit against the industry, and Alaska recently said it was seriously considering a lawsuit.
New York City and the California cities of San Francisco and San Jose and Los Angeles County also have joined in the battle.
Vacco said New York state's decision to take on the industry will have an impact on the nationwide litigation.
"The have the biggest player on the street involved in the these lawsuits now," he told a news conference.

If the state should prevail in its lawsuit, Vacco said the damages could be in the billions of dollars, making New York's earlier offer "seem like pocket change." The lawsuit, filed in state court in Manhattan, seeks unspecified damages.

In the 120-page complaint, he charged the companies under a racketeering law, accusing them of "conspiracy and racketeering in suppressing information about health and addiction in manipulating nicotine content and derailment of development of safer cigarettes and marketing tobacco products for minors."

Vacco said while other states had sued the industry's research arms -- the Washington-based Tobacco Institute and the New York-based Council for Tobacco Research USA Inc. -- the New York lawsuit is the first to seek their dissolution. He said this action was possible under state laws governing non-profit agencies. The Tobacco Institute said it would not comment on litigation.
Vacco said while the two groups were supposed to conduct impartial studies of the effects of tobacco, they were merely a "front for publicity" by providing misleading information to the public.

The filing of the lawsuit comes as Brooke Group Ltd. Chairman Bennett LeBow is seeking a settlement with all states that have filed Medicaid lawsuits against the tobacco industry in a deal that could involve the exchange of confidential documents.

Brooke is the parent of Liggett Group Inc., the first tobacco company to ever settle cigarette lawsuits. It shocked the financial community in March 1996 when it reached an accord with five states that sued the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers.

The lawsuit also comes when some state attorneys general and some plaintiffs lawyers also are seeking a possible legislative solution to the mounting litigation against the tobacco industry. The group has been meeting with intermediaries with contacts in the tobacco industry. So far, cigarette companies have denied any participation in the talks.
Vacco, however, said he did not file the lawsuit to try to get in on any settlement talks. He said he did not believe the industry wants to settle litigation.
Special Counsel Valente, who was on the state's negotiating team, said in an interview, "They had an attitude ... that they can't be beaten."
Some $2.6 billion is spent annually by private insurance companies and the Medicaid programme to treat smoking-related illness in New York.
